articles.title: Ti West’s Horror-Forward Ebenezer Is Haunted by an Overactive Johnny Depp Performance
articles.summary: Ti West’s Ebenezer does a respectable enough job taking a more horror-forward approach to A Christmas Carol, but the busy Johnny Depp performance at the heart of the film pulls more focus than is necessary.
articles.body:
One need only look to The Muppet Christmas Carol, the best Christmas movie of them all , to understand why Charles Dickens’ novella has endured countless adaptations over the nearly two hundred years since it was published. The miserly Ebenezer Scrooge’s confrontation with the ghosts of his past with hopes for a brighter future is so fundamentally strong that a staging of it by Michael Caine and Kermit the Frog that blends all sorts of tones and meta commentary has room not only to work, but to stand as an unambiguously respected adaptation of the text. Ti West’s Ebenezer feels most focused on illuminating the darker corners of Dickens’ tale, but the broad and classically Johnny Depp performance at its heart holds it back from ever elevating into a more meaningful adaptation of the text.

A Christmas Carol is, of course, a ghost story at its heart, and Ti West’s long history in the horror genre - including a ghost story of his own, The Innkeepers - makes him an interesting director to see paired with the material. West’s instincts on how and where to amp up A Christmas Carol’s spooky trappings are strong from the top down, and they’re most evident in Ebenezer’s production design. Ebenezer leans on the austere chill of its Victorian London setting well with practical sets and stages that instantly read as Christmas Carol-appropriate. The destitute and dour look of the film illuminates both the poverty Scrooge hates and the corresponding spiritual bankruptcy from which he suffers in equal measure. Tyler Bates’ string-heavy score helps to push that sense of unease, with the highlight piece being a driving and ominous string quartet version of “Carol of the Bells” played over the opening credits of Londoners bringing out decorations and getting ready for the approaching holiday.

While Ebenezer is largely a faithful adaptation of Dickens’ novella, West and writer Nathaniel Halpern embellish certain turns of the plot to underscore either Scrooge’s inner turmoil or the story’s horror elements, like adding a new prologue featuring Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen). The prologue serves the dual purpose of starting West’s darker take on the story off with a body (“Marley was dead: to begin with,” and all that) and giving McKellen just a little bit more time on camera. Formative events like Ebenezer’s tough childhood or his failed engagement with Belle get expounded on with enough care to work on their own merits, but with Depp’s Ebenezer tough to connect to emotionally, little of the new additions wind up feeling impactful enough to justify the time spent on them. Despite coming in just under two hours, each of the “staves” that Ebenezer is chaptered into routinely taper off in momentum before West is moving on to the next act of the story.

A director’s influence can only take Ebenezer Scrooge’s story so far. Any staging of A Christmas Carol lives and dies on the casting of its Scrooge: the whole story is told over Scrooge’s shoulder, and whatever catharsis the audience is able to experience through Scrooge’s own as he wakes up on Christmas Day a changed man has to be channeled through an accessible and readably human performance. That leaves Johnny Depp’s work here as Ebenezer Scrooge feeling like a frustrating misfire.

Depp’s Scrooge is a constant source of lively and unpredictable energy through the well-trodden events of Ebenezer’s story, it’s just not at all clear by the end of the film that it was the right energy for the more straightforward approach West employs throughout the rest of the film. Depp’s conception of Scrooge, with all of its physical business and explosive emotion, feels better suited to stage than screen. What’s all the more frustrating is that Depp is not only capable of stepping down the zaniness of his Scrooge when called on, but he’s far better in the role when doing so. The few moments throughout the film where Depp plays Scrooge with some reserve, like when trying to break through to his past selves to beg them to do things differently, connect pretty effectively, and the final stretch where Scrooge is able to rejoice in his overnight rebirth gives Depp’s manic approach to the character a better fitting context.

With Depp’s campy performance pushing Ebenezer’s otherwise macabre presentation to its breaking point, supporting players like Rupert Grint, Ellie Bamber, and Sam Claflin do a lot to keep the story grounded in more recognizable feelings. Grint’s affability as Scrooge’s clerk Bob Cratchit cuts Depp’s hissing negativity well, and Ebenezer could have used more of the genuine light that he and the Cracthit family contributes, if only for the contrast to make all of the film’s darkness feel that much more oppressive.

On that note, points to whoever was responsible for casting Freddie Lee-Grey as Tiny Tim: he has nary more to say than “god bless us, everyone”, but wow, does that kid step up to the plate and knock it out of the park when called to do so. As Scrooge’s nephew Fred, Claflin embodies the optimism and good nature that Scrooge detests with ease, with Daisy Ridley stopping by for what amounts to a cameo as Fred’s more skeptical wife Clara and walking away with one of the film’s bigger laughs. Bamber’s Belle is just as effective as Fred at portraying the warmth that Scrooge willingly and cruelly let go of years before.

West makes no attempt to give the spirits that visit Ebenezer any cheery or pleasant characteristics: they’re dead and they hate it, and from the looks of them, they have good reason to feel that way. McKellen’s Marley does get a brief moment to act as a canary in a moral coalmine for Scrooge early on, but he’s mostly here to lend some gravitas to the obligatory “you will be haunted by three spirits” moment, the kind of thing he’s been doing in his sleep for decades. Not helping his efforts at all are the cheap-looking visual effects doing the work to create McKellen’s spectral form. The poor quality of the visual effects extends to the dozens of nameless ghosts that arrive to put the fear of Father Christmas in Scrooge’s heart by banging on windows and going “ooh” and “ahh”, plaguing both he and the audience throughout the film.

Thankfully, the headliner Ghosts of Christmases Past, Present, and Yet to Come are better designed and realized. Andrea Riseborough’s bride-like Ghost of Christmas Past is the most outwardly eerie, with milky eyes and a detached, childlike voice which really cut through Depp’s bombast as Scrooge revisits a painful chapter of his younger days. Riseborough’s performance is monotone by design, but West supports Risebrough’s ethereal presence with some of the film’s more outwardly horror-coded cinematography, with some effective long takes that pull a sort of “Texas switch” by having her teleport quickly and creepily across long distances. Tramell Tillman’s Ghost of Christmas Present is more mercurial, and Tillman’s intensity and lack of patience with Scrooge’s waffling both give the sense that he could throttle Scrooge at the drop of a nightcap. The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come maintains the slow-moving, wordless and faceless presentation it usually does, but West at least gives it a haunting Predator-like clicking sound to set it apart.

articles.title: More game developers are starting to use generative AI
articles.summary: More video game developers are using generative AI tools in their jobs compared to last year, according to the GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey.
articles.body: More video game developers are using generative AI tools in their jobs compared to last year, according to the GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey. Forty percent of developers surveyed say they use it “as part of their job,” an increase from 36 percent in 2025. Usage was higher with game developers that work on free-to-play games at 58 percent and mobile-only studio workers at 70 percent. The survey is being published as the game industry continues to reckon with generative AI tools. While many game developers, particularly indie developers, have spoken out strongly against the technology, AI is at the center of indie awards conversations in part because Big Walk developer House House “sparingly” used LLMs to assist with technical challenges in the “final stretch” of development. AI is also increasingly being used to reverse-engineer retro games. And in a post on Thursday, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma seemed to indicate that AI will be central to Xbox’s future, saying that “A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars.” Seventy three percent of the survey’s respondents said they used AI for research and brainstorming, while 62 percent used it for data analysis and summarization, and 56 percent for code generation and debugging. Twenty two percent of respondents used generative AI for concept art or visual ideation, and 8 percent used it for production art or final game assets. The survey also included grim numbers about layoffs, with 34 percent of respondents saying they have been laid off sometime in the past two years.

articles.title: 25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
articles.summary: Microsoft is celebrating 25 years of Xbox, amid a giant restructuring. The future of Xbox feels more uncertain than ever before.
articles.body: Microsoft has spent the past 25 years trying to shake up the game console market. The original Xbox, which launched on November 15th in 2001, took on an industry dominated by Sony and Nintendo. Twenty-five years later, Xbox finds itself in a similar position. It’s not starting from scratch this time around, but to reach another 25-year milestone, it needs to do something radically different. The original Xbox was radically different. Born out of a fear of Sony putting a PC in the living room, Microsoft built its first game console around familiar PC technology. A custom Intel Pentium III processor powered the original Xbox, alongside an Nvidia GPU and 64MB of unified RAM. It was different from the fully custom architectures that Sony and Nintendo used at the time, allowing Microsoft to entice developers to its platform with tools that were more familiar to PC game makers. Microsoft also included two hardware features that were unusual for a console at the time: a built-in hard drive and Ethernet port. The hard drive let game developers cache content without having to rely fully on optical discs, and Xbox players could also use it for game saves without having to purchase a separate memory card. You could even rip CDs to an Xbox and listen to custom soundtracks while playing games. Xbox wasn’t the first to bring online gaming to consoles, but Microsoft took a different approach. Instead of relying on a built-in modem like Sega’s Dreamcast, Microsoft included an Ethernet port, anticipating a shift toward broadband internet connections. Xbox Live, which launched in November 2002, really nailed the entire online experience. There were friends lists, unique gamertags, voice chat through a bundled headset, and integrated multiplayer services. Microsoft created an entire platform for online gaming, making it easier for developers to support and fundamentally changing how people played games together. The Xbox 360 took these ideas a step further, with swappable hard drives, digital game downloads, wireless controllers, and backward compatibility. It also turned Microsoft’s game console into an entertainment hub for the living room, complete with streaming video apps. Kinect was perhaps its most radical addition. Launched in 2010, the motion-sensing device used cameras and microphones to let players control games with their bodies and voices. It quickly became the fastest-selling consumer electronics device in early 2011. But the success of Kinect and Microsoft’s ambition to turn Xbox into a home entertainment device helped lead to its first major strategic misstep with the Xbox One. Microsoft positioned the successor to the Xbox 360 around TV, entertainment, and an always-online future, instead of focusing on the games that had made Xbox successful. Its plans for online DRM and restrictions on used games sparked a huge backlash, while bundling Kinect pushed the console’s price $100 above Sony’s PlayStation 4. Six months after launch, Microsoft was forced to drop Kinect from the Xbox One console bundle to close that price gap. The Xbox One showed what happens when Microsoft loses sight of what gamers want. The company spent most of that generation playing catch-up to Sony’s impressive PlayStation 4 sales. But its weakened position also forced Microsoft to once again try something radically different with Xbox Game Pass. Introduced in 2017, Game Pass shook up the very economics of how people play games. The subscription service lets you access hundreds of games instead of buying them individually. Microsoft went on an acquisition spree to power its Game Pass ambitions, buying up smaller studios, Bethesda, and eventually Activision Blizzard. Game Pass has become one of Xbox’s most compelling features, but it has also raised difficult questions about the economics of putting all of Microsoft’s first-party games into a subscription service on day one. It has pleased Xbox fans, but Microsoft hasn’t demonstrated that it can turn the service into the mass-market success it once envisioned. Microsoft has also stopped regularly disclosing subscriber numbers, making it harder to judge if the service is growing or not. These days, Microsoft is spinning many Xbox plates. The Xbox Series X and S consoles that launched in 2020 are way behind Sony’s PS5 sales numbers, and Xbox Cloud Gaming hasn’t yet been able to reach the millions more players that Microsoft has always wanted for its ecosystem. Xbox Cloud Gaming promised to make games accessible on phones and tablets without needing a dedicated console, and combined with Microsoft’s messy project to bring Xbox games to PS5 and Nintendo consoles, the efforts have raised questions about what the Xbox brand actually represents these days. Microsoft hasn’t quite decided whether it wants to be a full third-party publisher, an ecosystem owner, or an unusual combination of both. Some of Microsoft’s recent radically different Xbox bets haven’t paid off, so it’s now turning its attention to a much smaller Xbox division, with a restructuring that will see overall Xbox headcount reduced by 20 percent by the end of Microsoft’s fiscal year in June 2027. “I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote in a message to Xbox employees today. Microsoft is celebrating 25 years of Xbox today with an event in Seattle for fans, where it’s launching Xbox Playback, a personalized look back at players’ 25-year Xbox history. There will be more fan-focused announcements throughout the day, but I’m not expecting any news on the next Xbox console. The celebration is awkwardly timed, because rumors have suggested that Microsoft is also preparing for more Xbox layoffs in November, during the same month it’s celebrating a milestone. The reset also comes as Microsoft is preparing for a next-generation Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, which will play both Xbox games and PC titles. It sounds like an effort to combine Windows and Xbox like never before. The next Xbox could also play every Xbox game ever made, thanks to Microsoft’s impressive bets on backward compatibility over the years. It’s an interesting full-circle moment. The original Xbox was essentially a PC built for the living room. Project Helix appears to be taking a similar approach, but this time around bringing the flexibility of PC gaming into a console experience. If Microsoft gets it right, it could open Xbox up to a much bigger library of games, and entice people trying to decide between a console or a gaming PC. The problem for Xbox is getting consumers to care about this next console, especially when its games are available on PC and sometimes on Sony’s and Nintendo’s platforms. “Xbox has the best console ecosystem around, packed with consumer-friendly features like free cloud saves, Game Pass, and my preferred controller,” says Jon Clarke, cofounder and editor-in-chief of DayOne. “None of these things are particularly sexy or flashy. They’re simply features that work, and that can make them difficult to get customers excited about.” Rebuilding the Xbox brand and launching a new console gives Microsoft an unusual opportunity to make another bold bet on the future, just like it did 25 years ago. But the risks this time around are greater, after more than a decade of trying and failing to catch up to the competition. “Up against competitors that have firmly established their place in the market, Xbox finds itself in a difficult position,” says Clarke. “Rebuilding the brand will be an expensive endeavor, and the bold ambition of combining the best of console gaming with the openness and flexibility of PC is easier said than done.” Xbox also needs good games, and after years of studio acquisitions it now has plenty of IP to play with. “Many of those franchises have lost their luster owing to years of mismanagement and potentially a generalized lack of vision,” says Jez Corden, executive editor at Windows Central. “Microsoft from the top will need to be willing to invest here to ensure Xbox’s franchises can not only find new audiences, but simply maintain what they already have.” Xbox also faces the challenge of RAMageddon’s impact on the hardware industry right now, pushing the prices of components beyond levels that consumers can comfortably afford. “If Xbox is to reclaim any of its former glory, innovating on the costs of the traditional video game ‘console’ will be absolutely paramount, otherwise it’s hard to imagine that it will continue to exist in its current form,” says Corden. A console projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 won’t grow the Xbox ecosystem. It could make more sense to let PC makers build their own Xbox hardware, opening up the platform to a wider range of prices and devices rather than relying on expensive flagship consoles. Twenty-five years ago, Microsoft built a PC and called it an Xbox. Now it’s preparing to build something that looks increasingly like a PC again, only this time it needs to convince people that it should still be called an Xbox. Microsoft has another opportunity to shake up the console industry, but its biggest challenge might be convincing players that Xbox needs to exist as a console at all. The pad * Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam. Protesters broke into the construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam earlier this week. Around 100 people made it into the site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.” There has been intense opposition to new data centers in Amsterdam, after the city banned new projects until 2030. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place. * Microsoft is reportedly “winding down” a cloud AI deal with Oracle. Bloomberg reports that Microsoft has been turning off rented capacity from Oracle, after declining to renew a 2023 deal. Oracle has been using older-generation Nvidia chips, reportedly making the renting deal less useful to the software maker. Microsoft is also reportedly reconsidering deals to rent server capacity from so-called “neoclouds” to power its AI efforts. * GTA VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming for Xbox One consoles. Microsoft and Rockstar Games have officially confirmed that Grand Theft Auto VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming next week, but there’s a pretty big catch. You’ll only be able to access the game using an Xbox Series S / X or Xbox One console. That’s unusual as you can normally stream Xbox Cloud Gaming titles to phones, PCs, TVs, tablets, and even web browsers. Microsoft also effectively has an exclusive on streaming Grand Theft Auto VI from the cloud for launch, albeit only to Xbox consoles. * Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode. Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs. The full release of Auto SR now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Previously, Auto SR was also limited to frame rates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit frame rates of up to 120fps. The new performance mode and compatibility with Auto HDR is rolling out through Windows updates. * Hackers are already exploiting an Outlook spoofing vulnerability. Microsoft is urging IT admins to install its latest Outlook patch this week, after it discovered a flaw that is being actively exploited. Hackers can send a specially crafted message to Outlook users that would force them to connect to an attacker-controlled network where authentication hashes could be stolen to impersonate users. Microsoft has marked this as moderate, but security researchers say a stolen hash can open the door to many other parts of a network, beyond just a mailbox. * Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now. Microsoft has ruled the productivity software world for decades with its own Office suite, but Anthropic unveiled new tools this week that are targeted at knowledge workers. Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards are all what they sound like, equivalents to Microsoft’s Office apps that join Claude Docs, Slides, and others. The tools are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical workers and are the latest AI-shaped warning shot against Microsoft’s Office empire. * Microsoft is bringing two popular Sysinternals tools to Linux and macOS. Linux users are getting a native version of Autoruns, the popular utility for managing what apps run at startup in Windows. Process Explorer, which is essentially a more powerful Task Manager, is also arriving on macOS. These are the latest Sysinternals tools to arrive on non-Windows platforms, as Neowin notes Sysmon, Procmon, and ProcDump are all available for Linux, and ZoomIt for macOS. * Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices are now available. At IFA earlier this year Microsoft and AMD both announced Project Zenith, a new “distraction-free Windows experience” for developers. This tweaked version of Windows 11 is now launching first on new AMD Ryzen AI Halo devices. You don’t need a whole new device to take advantage of the config tweaks of Project Zenith, as developers can use Microsoft’s Windows Developer Config from GitHub. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: New GTA 6 In-Game Footage Continues to Highlight the Game's Unbelievable Graphics
articles.summary: Rockstar has released yet another in-game clip from GTA 6, and like yesterday's footage, fans can't quite believe it's real.
articles.body:
Rockstar has released yet another in-game clip from GTA 6 , and like yesterday's footage, fans can't quite believe it's real.

This morning, the Instagram account "Only in Dade" (which posts real videos from around Miami, Florida) shared a video of several flashy cars driving around. However, this footage isn't real life; it's actually GTA 6 footage.

The page posted footage of these cars sitting on GTA 6's version of Ocean Drive yesterday while a group of NPCs observed them. Yesterday's footage was actually an in-game recreation of a real video that was posted in October, showing Rockstar's real-life marketing efforts in Miami. Presumably, the new video posted today is also a recreation of a real video from when the real versions of these cars were zooming around the city.

Although the footage doesn't show much, it is an extremely impressive showcase of GTA 6's graphical fidelity. When the first clip dropped yesterday, many thought it was AI or some kind of render. However, it has since been confirmed as authentic gameplay and was reposted by Rockstar itself on Instagram. Fans have reacted to both clips in awe of the visuals, noting that the game has really outdone itself.

"Absolutely insane this is in-game," said one fan in response to the new footage. "This game isn't real, bro; there HAS to be a trap somewhere. There is no f**king way," said another fan in disbelief .

Some have even joked that if this is really how the final game looks, they're more than happy to play it at 30fps . It's clear that Rockstar traded higher performance in favor of visual fidelity, and while that may not be what some fans want, it is inevitably going to result in one of the most graphically advanced games we have ever seen.

Today officially marks exactly one week until GTA 6's release. The game is available to preload right now and it is tracking to have one of the biggest launches in entertainment history. Xbox and PlayStation both confirmed that the game is the most preordered title in the history of their respective stores , and analysts have estimated that the game has already surpassed $1 billion in sales ahead of launch.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.body:
James Cameron isn't done with Avatar: Fire And Ash just yet. While a steelbook and standard 4Ks/Blu-rays released earlier this year, the film is now getting a four-disc Collector's Edition that's stacked with over 9 hours of bonus features. That's a real treat for fans of the film to dig into.

There's not long to wait for its release, either, as it's slated to drop on December 8. However, preorders like these can sell out fast. So, if you're eager to grab this new edition of the film and all its extra special features, head to the links below to preorder it for $74.99.

articles.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved to Get Firefight as a Free Update
articles.summary: When Halo: Campaign Evolved first came out in July it did not include any multiplayer modes, but the first-person shooter remake will at least get Firefight as a free update this Winter.
articles.body:
When Halo: Campaign Evolved first came out in July it did not include any multiplayer modes, but the first-person shooter remake will at least get Firefight as a free update this winter.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the returning mode in a social media post Thursday, along with a graphic showing a team of Spartans shooting a mix of Covenant and Flood enemies with various guns.

While Firefight isn't the arena competitive multiplayer that most fans had hoped from the Halo remake at launch, wave-based PvE has been a mainstay in the series since Halo 3: ODST in 2009. Essentially, you and your friends load into a map and fight increasingly difficult waves of enemies until you get overwhelmed. There's no reason to believe that this iteration is going to be any different.

Regardless of whether or not Team Deathmatch comes to Halo: Campaign Evolved, this will be the first multiplayer mode to hit the remake, which was pitched primarily as a straight-up revival of the iconic Combat Evolved campaign. Multiplayer was the major piece missing from Campaign Evolved, and this could be a sign that more multiplayer modes will be added in the future.

IGN's Halo: Combat Evolved remake gave it a 7 . We said: "Halo: Campaign Evolved speaks to the series' timelessness and adds a decent set of new missions, but it's a mostly a lean retread that's more of a test run for its future with Unreal Engine."

This Firefight announcement comes as Xbox celebrates its 25th anniversary. Earlier today, Sharma looked ahead, predicting "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations."

As for Halo, following the summer's drastic cuts at Microsoft's gaming business, Xbox announced a significant reshuffle that saw the next mainline Halo game handed to Call of Duty developer Activision , which is spinning up a new team to work on the franchise. Mass layoffs hit Halo Studios at the same time.

articles.title: Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds Are Credited as Writers on Avengers: Doomsday, Creating Speculation Over Deadpool and Wolverine Roles
articles.summary: Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds have been credited for contributing to Avengers: Doomsday's script, sall but confirming the return of Deadpool and Wolverine.
articles.body:
Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds have been credited for contributing to Avengers: Doomsday's script, all but confirming the return of Deadpool and Wolverine.

Per an update to the Writers Guild of America's website , Avengers: Doomsday has credited a handful of people for contributing to the film's script. Although the screenplay was written by Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron, the Additional Literary Material section confirms that Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Ryan Reynolds, and Hugh Jackman also contributed to the script. These credits are for people who are not the authors of the actual film's story, but helped punch up dialogue or did a small pass on the script.

With that said, Ryan Reynolds is well-known for helping write the Deadpool films, and it would be surprising for him to have helped out on this specific script if Deadpool wasn't in it. Although Hugh Jackman doesn't have a history as a writer, he may have also helped write Wolverine's scenes, as well, given he has spent 26 years playing the character.

The characters have been repeatedly teased to return in Doomsday by both Jackman and Reynolds, with the two doing tongue-in-cheek promos at San Diego Comic-Con and D23 over the summer. However, they haven't been explicitly confirmed to appear in the film. Since Deadpool and Wolverine were huge hits and fans have hoped to see the characters in an Avengers film for years, it only makes sense for them to finally crossover into the broader MCU.

Additionally, Spider-Man: Brand New Day director Destin Daniel Cretton also got a credit for Doomsday, but it's worth remembering he also directed Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings. Shang-Chi is confirmed to appear in the upcoming ensemble film, so it's more likely that his contributions are for helping write that character. It's possible Spider-Man is in the film, but it remains unclear at the moment.

Marvel also confirmed earlier this week that another major MCU character will return in Doomsday after a four-year absence. Scarlet Witch was seen at the end of VisionQuest being abducted by Doctor Doom, following her appearance in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. As a result, it seems like she may be an antagonist once again, though this time under the control of another character.
